items.title: Wendell Brunious interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: You know my dad always was a great musician, wrote for Billy Eckstine, Cab Calloway, Jay McShann, Walter Fats Pichon, and all these real bands.

ctx.x: This makes a case for jazz education going beyond the classroom, into what we call etiquette. Concert etiquette. But I want to say this about yourself, and then talk a little bit. I see you as being an important person, being a relatively young man, from New Orleans, restoring some of the respect of the music and the tradition. Do you see — where do you see yourself?

Well I don’t feel I am respected enough. Like I don’t think people look at me as real important. I really don’t. Because I don’t know, I’m not one of these real ultra contemporary neo jazz guys. You know what I mean? I’m very much a pretty conservative musician. You know my dad always was a great musician, wrote for Billy Eckstine, Cab Calloway, Jay McShann, Walter Fats Pichon, and all these real bands. You know? And he just taught us to do what was right. Just follow your heart. Do what’s right man. And a lot of…

now. I teach at the University of New Orleans. And the response I get from a lot of these kids is like, oh yeah, well you’re playing old time, or something like that. I mean I’m pretty much a New Orleans and kind of more like a Bebop trumpet player. Which I mean Bebop had the feeling, you know still had the feeling. With all of these modes like Dan was explaining, man, you know I don’t feel that. You know it’s very, very like intellectual. Really like, wow man, that guy must really know some really high-powered…

items.title: Wendell Brunious interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 16, 2000 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: he started touring with, I think it was the Jay McShann band at first.

ctx.x: Who has the Olympia Brass Band. That was my dad’s first cousin. And he went up there and he auditioned for Juilliard and he won a scholarship to Juilliard. So when he was 16 he was at Juilliard. And by the time he was 19, I don’t know if he had graduated or if he had left, I don’t know what the thing was, but my mom’s mother had died so he came back to New Orleans, they got married, and he started touring with, I think it was the Jay McShann band at first. And he wrote some arrangements, Charlie Parker was in the…
Oh gee, I didn’t know that.
